nodes.label: Item semantics
nodes.summary: Preserves the geometry of semantic item IDs when adding them to an LLM vocabulary. Initializing tokens from their semantic centroids improves learning efficiency and recommendation for less frequent items.

nodes.label: PauseRec
nodes.summary: Studies why explicit reasoning can struggle with semantic item IDs. PauseRec uses implicit reasoning to reduce the training and inference costs of LLM-based generative recommendation.

nodes.label: SnapLGR
nodes.summary: Brings LLM-based generative retrieval to short-video recommendation. The system combines graph-informed semantic IDs, vocabulary grounding, and efficient serving.

nodes.label: LLM memorization
nodes.summary: Finds that much of the gain from LLM recommenders comes from memorizing one-step item transitions. IIRG trains richer collaborative and semantic item relationships to improve generalization.

nodes.label: ID + text
nodes.summary: Shows that item-ID and text-based recommenders capture complementary signals. Independently training and then combining the two models provides a simple way to preserve those strengths.

nodes.label: CoRRe
nodes.summary: Refines LLM-generated item representations with collaborative information after the LLM runs. Co-purchase structure shapes embedding directions, while popularity adjusts their magnitudes.

nodes.label: Weight decay
nodes.summary: Explains how weight decay encodes item popularity in embedding magnitudes. PRISM initializes that information directly, simplifying collaborative-filtering training and offering control over popularity bias.

nodes.label: Matrix rank
nodes.summary: Connects collaborative-filtering losses to the stable rank of embedding tables. Regularizing rank early in training improves optimization and can reduce reliance on expensive negative sampling.

nodes.label: GraphHash
nodes.summary: Uses communities in the user–item interaction graph to share embeddings. This graph-informed hashing reduces memory while preserving useful collaborative information.

nodes.label: GaLA
nodes.summary: Explains how serializing a graph can suppress attention between its neighbors in an LLM. GaLA adjusts attention at inference time to better preserve graph relationships.

nodes.label: GLANCE
nodes.summary: Learns when a graph model should request LLM assistance. A node-aware router uses local structural signals to target the nodes that benefit from the extra information.

nodes.label: PENCIL
nodes.summary: Uses a plain Transformer over sampled local subgraphs for link prediction. Attention captures structural signals without elaborate hand-built encodings or large node-ID tables.

nodes.label: Edge automorphism
nodes.summary: Quantifies when GNNs cannot distinguish structurally equivalent links. EO-GNN uses orbit-aware designs to improve link prediction while retaining equivariance.

nodes.label: MAGNET
nodes.summary: Treats multi-agent task assignment as learning over edges of a bipartite graph. A line-graph transformation, pruning, and feasibility checks combine learned scoring with assignment constraints.

nodes.label: Local performance
nodes.summary: Shows that node performance depends on how local homophily differs from the overall graph. Aggregate accuracy can conceal systematic failures on underrepresented neighborhoods.

nodes.label: Local fairness
nodes.summary: Frames underrepresented local homophily as an out-of-distribution fairness problem. Theory and new benchmarks show how neighborhood structure can affect predictions across sensitive groups.

nodes.label: Neighborhood fairness
nodes.summary: Connects local neighborhood assortativity to group fairness. GNN designs that handle heterophilous neighborhoods can improve treatment of otherwise disadvantaged groups.

nodes.label: FairEdit
nodes.summary: Adds and removes graph edges to improve prediction fairness. Its gradient-guided editing approach works with different GNN models.

nodes.label: Network design
nodes.summary: Shows that structural biases can mislead gradient-based graph editing. ORE repeatedly edits and re-embeds a graph to refresh the information guiding the next change.

nodes.label: Heterophily + robustness
nodes.summary: Connects graph homophily to adversarial vulnerability. Separating ego-node and neighbor representations can improve robustness as well as learning on heterophilous graphs.

nodes.label: Reliable explanations
nodes.summary: Studies how adversarial training changes the reliability of GNN explanations. It also evaluates whether explanations reflect learned representations and recover meaningful chemistry insights.

nodes.label: Counterfactuals
nodes.summary: Uses a generative model to make meaningful changes to images and examine how a classifier responds. These interventions expose what can change a prediction.

nodes.label: Actionable attribution
nodes.summary: Introduces domain-specific concepts as controllable inputs to model interpretation. Generative modeling helps turn explanations into actionable scientific questions.

nodes.label: Molecular density
nodes.summary: Predicts crystalline density from molecular chemical structure. A comparison of learned graph representations and fixed features also investigates what the models learn.

nodes.label: Zeroth-order SciML
nodes.summary: Connects scientific software to neural-network training without requiring a differentiable simulator. Gradient-free optimization brings domain knowledge into data-limited materials tasks.

nodes.label: Material strength
nodes.summary: Predicts the compressive strength of molecular solids from microscope images. It compares engineered visual features and learned features across different data regimes.

nodes.label: Crystal packing
nodes.summary: Introduces Autopack to identify molecular-crystal packing motifs using representative neighboring molecules. Automated labels enable larger studies of composition and crystal organization.

nodes.label: Active galaxies
nodes.summary: Tests whether an emission-line width can stand in for stellar velocity dispersion in active galaxies. This early astronomy study is shown separately from the connected machine-learning threads.

edges.label: Embedding geometry
edges.reason: Both explain collaborative-filtering training through embedding geometry: stable rank in one case, popularity encoded in vector magnitudes in the other.

edges.label: Scaling embedding tables
edges.reason: Both target the cost of large recommender embeddings. Rank regularization addresses training cost; GraphHash addresses memory through shared embeddings.

edges.label: Popularity in vector magnitudes
edges.reason: The weight-decay study explains popularity in embedding magnitudes; CoRRe explicitly uses item popularity to refine magnitudes after LLM representation generation.

edges.label: What initialization encodes
edges.reason: Both change what recommendation embeddings encode at initialization: PRISM injects popularity information, while semantic initialization preserves item meaning that random initialization loses.

edges.label: Preserving item meaning
edges.reason: Both preserve useful item meaning alongside behavioral information: through ID–text model combinations in sequential recommendation, and semantic token initialization in generative recommendation.

edges.label: Combining semantic and collaborative signals
edges.reason: Both preserve useful information from separate signals before combining them. ID–text ensembling joins independently trained models; CoRRe refines LLM representations with collaborative signals.

edges.label: Beyond a single recommendation signal
edges.reason: Both find value in combining semantic and behavioral relationships. One studies ID–text complementarity; the other trains LLMs on richer item relationships beyond one-step transitions.

edges.label: Semantic IDs meet pretrained LLMs
edges.reason: Both examine the mismatch between new item tokens and a pretrained LLM. One changes token initialization; the other changes recommendation reasoning.

edges.label: Grounding an item vocabulary
edges.reason: Both address an LLM’s new item vocabulary. Semantic initialization preserves token geometry; SnapLGR combines semantic IDs with vocabulary-grounding training for production retrieval.

edges.label: Richer item relationships
edges.reason: Both use item relationships beyond a single interaction. SnapLGR adds co-engagement information to its semantic IDs; IIRG trains collaborative and semantic relations to improve generalization.

edges.label: Graphs inform item representations
edges.reason: Both use interaction-graph structure when constructing item representations. GraphHash clusters users and items for shared embeddings; SnapLGR adds co-engagement information to semantic IDs.

edges.label: Using what an LLM knows
edges.reason: Both ask why an LLM recommender may fail to use its pretrained knowledge effectively. One studies memorization; the other examines explicit versus implicit reasoning.

edges.label: Collaborative structure before ranking
edges.reason: Both extract useful structure from interaction graphs. GraphHash uses graph communities to share embeddings; CoRRe uses co-purchase neighbors to refine item representations.

edges.label: LLMs that respect graph structure
edges.reason: Both adapt language-model use to graph structure. GLANCE decides which nodes need LLM assistance; GaLA modifies attention to retain graph adjacency during reasoning.

edges.label: Attention over graph structure
edges.reason: Both investigate how Transformers represent graph relationships. PENCIL learns from local subgraphs; GaLA corrects attention distortion when graphs are serialized for an LLM.

edges.label: Distinguishing candidate links
edges.reason: Both study structural expressiveness for link prediction. PENCIL uses local-subgraph attention; the edge-automorphism framework quantifies indistinguishable links and motivates an orbit-aware GNN.

edges.label: Learning over edges
edges.reason: Both make edge representations central to the learning task. EO-GNN distinguishes structural link roles; MAGNET scores agent–task assignments through a line-graph transformation.

edges.label: Learning to change a network
edges.reason: Both use learned graph information for decisions over edges. MAGNET selects feasible assignments; ORE edits graph structure while refreshing the gradients used to guide changes.

edges.label: Two uses of bipartite structure
edges.reason: Both exploit bipartite graphs, in different applications. MAGNET transforms agent–task graphs for assignment; GraphHash clusters user–item graphs to reduce embedding memory.

edges.label: Local homophily as distribution shift
edges.reason: Both examine nodes whose local homophily differs from the graph overall. The performance study diagnoses accuracy gaps; the fairness study analyzes unequal outcomes across sensitive groups.

edges.label: Fairness depends on the neighborhood
edges.reason: Both connect local homophily to unfair predictions. The later study adds an out-of-distribution formulation and benchmarks for underrepresented neighborhood patterns.

edges.label: Helping overlooked node subgroups
edges.reason: Both examine outcomes hidden by graph-wide averages. Local-fairness analysis studies underrepresented neighborhoods; GLANCE routes assistance according to where a GNN needs help.

edges.label: Where a graph model struggles
edges.reason: The local-performance study identifies accuracy gaps across neighborhood patterns. GLANCE uses local structural signals to decide when an LLM can help a GNN.

edges.label: Homophily-sensitive model design
edges.reason: Both explain why neighborhood similarity affects GNN behavior. One analyzes local accuracy gaps; the other connects heterophily-aware designs to adversarial robustness.

edges.label: Diagnosing and improving graph fairness
edges.reason: Both address fairness in node prediction. The neighborhood study analyzes structural causes; FairEdit changes graph edges to improve fairness.

edges.label: Gradient-guided graph editing
edges.reason: Both use gradients to choose graph edits. FairEdit optimizes fairness; the network-design study examines structural biases in these gradients and proposes iterative re-embedding.

edges.label: Robustness and model understanding
edges.reason: Both examine adversarial behavior in GNNs. One studies structural attacks and robust architectures; the other studies how adversarial training affects explanation reliability.

edges.label: Can we trust model-derived importance?
edges.reason: Both examine whether information extracted from a GNN is meaningful. One tests gradients used for editing; the other evaluates explanations of learned representations.

edges.label: Understanding molecular graph models
edges.reason: Both investigate what graph models learn about chemistry. The density study compares learned and fixed representations; the explanation study examines reliable domain-relevant insights.

edges.label: Explanations that help scientific inquiry
edges.reason: Both seek useful scientific understanding from learned models. Reliable GNN explanations focus on training and faithfulness; actionable attribution uses domain concepts to guide interventions.

edges.label: Generative interventions for explanation
edges.reason: Both use generative models to make meaningful input changes and inspect predictions. Actionable attribution brings domain-specific scientific concepts into this intervention-based approach.

edges.label: Interpreting material microstructure
edges.reason: The strength study predicts material properties from microscope images; actionable attribution studies how meaningful changes to scientific inputs can reveal useful model behavior.

edges.label: Putting domain knowledge into learning
edges.reason: Both connect scientific knowledge to neural models. Actionable attribution uses domain concepts for interpretation; zeroth-order SciML incorporates scientific software into training.

edges.label: From molecular structure to crystal properties
edges.reason: Both examine molecular materials through structure. The density study predicts a bulk property from chemical structure; Autopack measures how molecules organize in crystals.

edges.label: Learning material properties from representations
edges.reason: Both compare ways to represent materials for property prediction. One uses molecular graphs and chemical features; the other uses learned and engineered microscope-image features.

edges.label: Learning with limited scientific data
edges.reason: Both study materials prediction with limited data. The density work evaluates representations; zeroth-order SciML adds scientific knowledge through black-box software.

edges.label: Characterizing crystalline materials
edges.reason: Both extract information about the organization of molecular solids. Autopack labels molecular packing; the strength study learns useful information from microscopy.

edges.label: Preserving structure at the LLM interface
edges.reason: Both examine information lost at the LLM interface: graph adjacency during serialization, and semantic geometry when initializing new item tokens.
